title: Nana Fadnavis and the Twelve Pillars

title_i18n.en: Nana Fadnavis and the Twelve Pillars

subtitle: How a cautious minister held a storm-tossed throne for a child Peshwa
era: Barabhai Council and late Confederacy diplomacy, 1773-1800 CE
region: Pune, Salbai, Wadgaon, Delhi and the Deccan courts
moral: Patient diplomacy can hold a fragile house together.

sources.citation: Peshwa Daftar, Nana Fadnavis letters, roznishi and diplomatic dispatches
sources.note: Large primary archive for late Maratha governance and intelligence.

sources.citation: Treaty of Wadgaon, 1779, and Treaty of Salbai, 1782, in British and Maratha records
sources.note: Documented instruments marking First Anglo-Maratha War outcomes.

sources.citation: Prachi Deshpande, Creative Pasts (Columbia UP, 2007); Stewart Gordon, The Marathas 1600-1818
sources.note: Modern interpretations of Nana's memory, diplomacy and limitations.

panels.shot: low-angle mid-shot in dim court

dialogue.text: In the age of gunpowder and Company gold, Nana Fadnavis guarded a child’s throne and tried to bind a restless Maratha confederacy with paper, patience and fear.

panels.shot: wide interior of Shaniwar Wada with deep perspective

dialogue.text: In 1773, Shaniwar Wada shook. Peshwa Narayanrao lay dead, his blood-feud leaving no clear heir, only fear in the courtyards of Pune.

panels.shot: slow push-in on Nana at a low lamp-lit desk

dialogue.text: Nana, son of a Deshastha family risen through service, was already keeper of accounts and letters. The Daftar was his battlefield, ink his chosen sword.

panels.shot: council-table wide shot with figures half in shadow

dialogue.text: Out of the crisis rose the Barabhai, the ‘twelve brothers’. Old houses of the Confederacy shared power, agreeing that the infant Madhavrao II would sit as Peshwa in name.

panels.shot: medium shot of Nana beside a cradle-throne

dialogue.text: A child was placed on the gaddi. Behind him, elders guarded their own claims. Nana, one among them, took the task of shielding the boy and the fragile prestige of Pune.

panels.shot: overhead view of Deccan map and scattered letters

dialogue.text: Beyond Pune, the Confederacy stretched in long arcs: Scindia in the north, Bhonsles in Nagpur, Gaekwads in Baroda, Holkars in Malwa, and new sultans and Europeans watching from every horizon.

panels.shot: medium shot at balcony overlooking Pune street

dialogue.text: To the west, the English Company crept inland with counting-houses and forts. They spoke as traders, but moved like rulers, measuring every fissure in Maratha politics.

panels.shot: tense council close-wide inside Shaniwar Wada

dialogue.text: When disputes tore the Barabhai, some sought English help. Nana feared that once foreign troops entered Deccan quarrels, they would never leave.

panels.shot: wide shot of Maratha camp outside Wadgaon hills

dialogue.text: War came in 1779. At Wadgaon, British forces were outmaneuvered in the ghats. The Treaty that followed forced them to restore their gains and humbled their Pune agents.

panels.shot: medium interior shot of Nana negotiating with a British officer

dialogue.text: Yet victory brought choice. Some Marathas wanted harsher terms. Nana and his colleagues weighed gains against future storms from Bombay and Calcutta.

panels.shot: slow push-in on Nana’s thoughtful profile

dialogue.speaker: nana_fadnavis
dialogue.text: Steel wins a field, but words decide how long we keep it.

panels.shot: wide diplomatic durbar with multiple envoys

dialogue.text: The First Anglo-Maratha War dragged on. Across years, diplomacy stretched as long as campaigns. Each letter weighed alliance with Scindia, Bhonsle, even Mysore, against the Company’s hunger.

panels.shot: map-table shot focused on Salbai region

dialogue.text: In 1782, the Treaty of Salbai was sealed. It confirmed Raghunathrao’s claims set aside, fixed frontiers, and brought a wary peace between the Peshwa’s court and the English Company.

panels.shot: medium shot of Nana in correspondence with Scindia’s envoy

dialogue.text: To the north, Mahadji Scindia carved power around Delhi, placing puppet emperors and minting his own strength. Nana’s letters to him show alliance, rivalry and endless bargaining over prestige and revenue.

panels.shot: wide shot of council arguing about Mysore

dialogue.text: In the south, Haidar Ali and Tipu Sultan challenged both Maratha and English claims. Some in Pune wanted firmer war, others trade. Nana’s caution sometimes meant lost chances and new resentments.

panels.shot: dim corridor shot of Nana passing restless soldiers

dialogue.text: Colonial chroniclers later called him ‘Machiavellian’. His own records show something slower: a minister balancing factions, sometimes delaying decisions, sometimes letting chances rot rather than risk collapse.

panels.shot: quiet interior with Nana teaching the young Peshwa

dialogue.text: He tried to school his Peshwa in ledgers and limits, not only battles. But a throne bound by elders is a throne chafing to be free.

panels.shot: somber court with news of Madhavrao II’s death

dialogue.text: When Madhavrao II died in 1795, whispers of poison and despair filled Pune. The Barabhai’s long guardianship ended in grief, not in the stable kingship they had hoped for.

panels.shot: late-life close-up with piles of ageing documents

dialogue.text: By the late 1790s, new strongmen like Daulat Rao Scindia and the English governors eyed Pune. Nana’s influence waned, his body slowing as the tempo of conquest quickened.

panels.shot: low-angle shot of Shaniwar Wada as storm clouds gather

dialogue.text: Nana died in 1800, just before the Second Anglo-Maratha War. Within a few years, British troops would march where his letters once ruled, and the Peshwa’s power would unravel.

panels.shot: final reflective close-up of a sealed Daftar bundle

dialogue.text: His papers, surviving in the Peshwa Daftar, show no lone mastermind, but a careful minister who, with others, held a divided confederacy together for a generation by diplomacy more than by sword.
